Name: What is an IP address and an Octet?

ContentBlocks.TextContent: <FlowDocument FontSize="14" Foreground="#FFFFFFFF" Background="#FF1A1A1A" TextAlignment="Left" FlowDirection="LeftToRight" ColumnWidth="Auto" IsOptimalParagraphEnabled="False" PageWidth="Auto" PageHeight="Auto" PagePadding="5,0,5,0" IsHyphenationEnabled="False" AllowDrop="True" NumberSubstitution.CultureSource="User" xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"><Paragraph Margin="0,0,0,0" Padding="0,0,0,0" TextAlignment="Left" FlowDirection="LeftToRight" LineHeight="Auto" Foreground="#FFFFFFFF"><Run BaselineAlignment="Baseline" FlowDirection="LeftToRight" Foreground="#FFFFFFFF" xml:space="preserve">What an IP Address Really IsAn IPv4 address is a 32-bit number used to identify a device on a network.Because 32 bits is hard to read, it’s broken into four 8-bit sections.Why It’s Called an OctetOctet = 8 bits8 bits can represent 256 values (0–255)IPv4 = 4 octets × 8 bits = 32 bitsExample:192.168.214.37Octet	Binary	Decimal192	11000000	Network168	10101000	Network214	11010110	Network37	00100101	DeviceThe term octet exists because not all systems historically used 8-bit bytes — “octet” removes ambiguity.Network vs Device (Street Address Analogy)Think of an IP like a mailing address:192.168.214.37192.168.214 → Street37 → House numberIf two devices are not on the same “street,” they cannot talk directly.Your Two Networks (Critical)192.168.214.x → Network A192.168.213.x → Network BEven though they look similar, 214 ≠ 213That single number change means different networks.</Run></Paragraph></FlowDocument>
